nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a number field with basis $B=\{b_1,\dots,b_n\}$ and let $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n$ be the embeddings of $K$ into $\CC$. Now let $M$ be the matrix \[\left (\begin{matrix} \sigma_1(b_1) &\cdots& \sigma_1(b_n)\\ \vdots & & \vdots \\ \sigma_n(b_1) &\cdots& \sigma_n(b_n) \end{matrix} \right ).\] Then \[\Delta(B)=\det(M)^2.\]
nodes.name: Discriminant via embeddings
nodes.statement_short: The discriminant of a basis equals $\det(M)^2$, $M$ the matrix of embeddings applied to the basis.
assumptions: $K$ be a number field with basis $B=\{b_1,\dots,b_n\}$
nodes.label: lemma:disc_via_embs

nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lemma:alt_definition_of_trace} we know that $\Tr_{K/\QQ}(b_i b_j)= \sum_k \sigma_k(b_i)\sigma_k(b_j)$ which is the same as the $(i,j)$ entry of $M^t M$. Therefore \[\det(T_B)=\det(M^t M)=\det(M)^2.\]
nodes.name: Proof of Discriminant via embeddings
nodes.statement_short: Express traces via embeddings, so the trace matrix is $M^tM$; take determinants.

nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a number field and $B=\{1,\a,\a^2,\dots,\a^{n-1}\}$ for some $\a \in K$. Then \[\Delta(B)=\prod_{i < j} (\sigma_i(\a)-\sigma_j(\a))^2\] where $\sigma_i$ are the embeddings of $K $ into $\CC$. Here $\Delta(B)$ denotes the discriminant.
nodes.name: Discriminant of a power basis
nodes.statement_short: Discriminant of the power basis of $\a$ is the squared Vandermonde product of its conjugates.
assumptions: $K$ be a number field and $B=\{1,\a,\a^2,\dots,\a^{n-1}\}$ for some $\a \in K$
nodes.label: lemma:disc_of_prim_elt_basis

nodes.statement: First we recall a classical linear algebra result relating to the Vandermonde matrix, which states that \[\det \left (\begin{matrix} 1 & x_1& x_1^2&\cdots&x_1^{n-1} \\ \vdots & & & \vdots \\ 1 & x_n& x_n^2&\cdots&x_n^{n-1} \end{matrix} \right ) =\prod_{i<j} (x_i-x_j).\] Combining this with Lemma \ref{lemma:disc_via_embs} gives the result.
nodes.name: Proof of Discriminant of a power basis
nodes.statement_short: Vandermonde determinant combined with the embedding formula for the discriminant.

nodes.statement: Let $f$ be a monic irreducible polynomial over a number field $K$ and let $\a$ be one of its roots in $\CC$. Then \[f'(\a)=\prod_{\beta \neq \a} (\a-\beta), \] where the product is over the roots of $f$ different from $\a$.
nodes.name: Derivative of an irreducible polynomial at a root
assumptions: $f$ be a monic irreducible polynomial over a number field $K$
$\a$ be one of its roots in $\CC$
nodes.label: lemma:diff_of_irr_pol

nodes.statement: We first write $f(x)=(x-\a)g(x)$ which we can do (over $\CC$) as $\a$ is a root of $f$, where now $g(x)=\prod_{\beta \neq \a} (x-\beta)$. Differentiating we get \[f'(x)=g(x)+(x-\a)g'(x).\] If we now evaluate at $\a$ we get the result.
nodes.name: Proof of Derivative of an irreducible polynomial at a root
nodes.statement_short: Factor $f(x)=(x-\a)g(x)$, differentiate by the product rule and evaluate at $\a$.

nodes.statement: Let $K=\QQ(\a)$ be a number field with $n=[K:\QQ]$ and let $B=\{1,\a,\a^2,\dots,\a^{n-1}\}$. Then \[\Delta(B)=(-1)^{\frac{n(n-1)}{2}}N_{K/\QQ}(m_\a'(\a))\] where $m_\a'$ is the derivative of $m_\a(x)$ (which we recall denotes the minimal polynomial of $\a$).
nodes.name: Discriminant of a power basis via norm of derivative
nodes.statement_short: Power-basis discriminant equals $\pm N_{K/\QQ}(m_\a'(\a))$ with sign $(-1)^{n(n-1)/2}$.
assumptions: $K=\QQ(\a)$ be a number field with $n=[K:\QQ]$
nodes.label: lemma:num_field_disc_in_terms_of_norm

nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lemma:disc_of_prim_elt_basis} we have $\Delta(B)=\prod_{i < j}(\a_i-\a_j)^2$ where $\a_k:=\sigma_k(\a)$. Next, we note that the number of terms in this product is $1+2+\cdots+(n-1)=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$. So if we write each term as $(\a_i-\a_j)^2=-(\a_i-\a_j)(\a_j-\a_i)$ we get \[\Delta(B)=(-1)^{\frac{n(n-1)}{2}}\prod_{i=1}^n \prod_{i \neq j} (\a_i-\a_j). \] Now, by lemmas \ref{lemma:diff_of_irr_pol} and \ref{lemma:alt_definition_of_norm} we see that \[N_{K/\QQ}(m_\a'(\a))=\prod_{i=1}^n m_\a'(\a_i)=\prod_{i=1}^n \prod_{i \neq j} (\a_i-\a_j),\] which gives the result.
nodes.name: Proof of Discriminant of a power basis via norm of derivative
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the squared Vandermonde product with a sign count, then identify it as the norm of $m_\a'(\a)$ via conjugates.

nodes.statement: Let $\zeta_p$ be a $p$-th root of unity for $p$ an odd prime, let $\lam_p=1-\zeta_p$ and $K=\QQ(\zeta_p)$. Then \[\Delta(\{1,\zeta_p,\dots,\zeta_p^{p-2}\})=\Delta(\{1,\lam_p,\dots,\lam_p^{p-2}\})=(-1)^{\frac{(p-1)}{2}}p^{p-2}.\]
nodes.name: Discriminant of the p-th cyclotomic field
nodes.statement_short: Discriminant of the power bases in $\zeta_p$ and $\lambda_p$ is $(-1)^{(p-1)/2}p^{p-2}$.
assumptions: $\zeta_p$ be a $p$-th root of unity for $p$ an odd prime
$\lam_p=1-\zeta_p$ and $K=\QQ(\zeta_p)$
nodes.label: lem:discr_of_cyclo

nodes.statement: First note $[K:\QQ]=p-1$. Since $\zeta_p=1-\lam_p$ we at once get $\ZZ[\zeta_p]=\ZZ[\lam_p]$ (just do double inclusion). Next, let $\a_i=\sigma_i(\zeta_p)$ denote the conjugates of $\zeta_p$, which is the same as the image of $\zeta_p$ under one of the embeddings $\sigma_i: \QQ(\zeta_p) \to \CC$. Now by Proposition \ref{lemma:disc_of_prim_elt_basis} we have \begin{align*}\Delta(\{1,\zeta_p,\dots,\zeta_p^{p-2}\})=\prod_{i < j} (\a_i-\a_j)^2 &=\prod_{i < j} ((1-\a_i)-(1-\a_j))^2\\&=\Delta(\{1,\lam_p,\dots,\lam_p^{p-2}\})\end{align*} Now, by Proposition \ref{lemma:num_field_disc_in_terms_of_norm}, we have \[\Delta(\{1,\zeta_p,\cdots,\zeta_p^{p-2}\})=(-1)^{\frac{(p-1)(p-2)}{2}}N_{K/\QQ}(\Phi_p'(\zeta_p) )\] Since $p$ is odd $(-1)^{\frac{(p-1)(p-2)}{2}}=(-1)^{\frac{(p-1)}{2}}$. Next, we see that \[\Phi_p'(x)=\frac{px^{p-1}(x-1)-(x^p-1)}{(x-1)^2}\] therefore \[\Phi_p'(\zeta_p)=-\frac{p\zeta_p^{p-1}}{\lam_p}.\] Lastly, note that $N_{K/\QQ}(\zeta_p)=1$, since this is the constant term in its minimal polynomial. Similarly, we see $N_{K/\QQ}(\lam_p)=p$. Putting this all together, we get \[N_{K/\QQ}(\Phi_p'(\zeta_p) )=\frac{N_{K/\QQ}(p)N_{K\QQ}(\zeta_p)^{p-1}}{N_{K/\QQ}(-\lam_p)}=(-1)^{p-1}p^{p-2}=p^{p-2}\]
nodes.name: Proof of Discriminant of the p-th cyclotomic field
nodes.statement_short: Direct computation: change variables $\zeta_p\mapsto\lambda_p$, then use the norm-of-derivative formula. The key step computes $\Phi_p'(\zeta_p)=-p\zeta_p^{p-1}/\lambda_p$ and the norms of $\zeta_p$, $\lambda_p$.

nodes.statement: We need to prove is that $\OO_K=\ZZ[\zeta_p]$. The inclusion $\ZZ[\zeta_p] \subseteq \OO_K$ is obvious. Let now $x \in \OO_K$. By Lemma \ref{lemma:disc_int_basis} and Proposition \ref{lem:discr_of_cyclo}, there is $k \in \NN$ such that $p^k x \in \ZZ[\zeta_p]$. We conclude by Lemma \ref{lemma:eis_crit_and_alg_ints}.

nodes.statement_short: Discriminant bound gives $p^kx\in\ZZ[\zeta_p]$; conclude with the Eisenstein criterion lemma.

nodes.statement: Let $p \geq 5$ be an prime number, $\zeta_p$ a $p$-th root of unity and $x, y \in \ZZ$ coprime. For $i \neq j$ with $i,j \in {0,\dots,p-1}$ we can write \[(\zeta_p^i-\zeta_p^j)=u(1-\zeta_p)\] with $u$ a unit in $\ZZ[\zeta_p]$. From this it follows that the ideals \[(x+y),(x+\zeta_py),(x+\zeta_p^2y),\dots,(x+\zeta_p^{p-1}y)\] are pairwise coprime.
nodes.section: 4 Fermat's Last Theorem for regular primes
nodes.name: Pairwise coprimality of the ideals x + zeta^i y
nodes.statement_short: For coprime $x,y$, the ideals $(x+\zeta_p^i y)$ are pairwise coprime.
assumptions: $p \geq 5$ be an prime number, $\zeta_p$ a $p$-th root of unity and $x, y \in \ZZ$ coprime
nodes.label: lem:flt_ideals_coprime

nodes.statement: Lemma \ref{lemma:zeta_pow_sub_eq_unit_zeta_sub_one} gives that $u$ is a unit. So all that needs to be proved is that the ideals are coprime. Assume not, then for some $i \neq j$ we have some prime ideal $\gothp$ dividing by $(x+y\zeta_p^i)$ and $(x+y\zeta_p^j)$. It must then also divide their sum and their difference, so we must have $\gothp | (1-\zeta_p)$ or $\gothp | y$. Similarly, $\gothp$ divides $\zeta_p^j(x+y\zeta_p^i)-\zeta_p^i(x+y\zeta_p^j)$ so $\gothp$ divides $x$ or $(1-\zeta_p)$. We can't have $\gothp$ dividing $x,y$ since they are coprime, therefore $\gothp |(1-\zeta_p)$. We know that since $(1-\zeta_p)$ has norm $p$ it must be a prime ideal, so $\gothp=(1-\zeta_p)$. Now, note that $x+y \equiv x+y\zeta_p^i \equiv 0 \mod \gothp$. But since $x,y \in \ZZ$ this means we would have $x+y \equiv 0 \pmod p$, which implies $z^p \equiv 0 \pmod p$ which contradicts our assumptions.
nodes.section: 4 Fermat's Last Theorem for regular primes
nodes.name: Proof of Pairwise coprimality of the ideals x + zeta^i y
nodes.statement_short: By contradiction: a common prime factor must be $(1-\zeta_p)$, which forces $p\mid x+y$ and hence $p\mid z$.

nodes.statement: Looking at $\a=a_0+a_1\zeta_p+\cdots+a_{p-1}\zeta_p^{p-1}$, if one of the $a_i$'s is zero and $\a/n \in \ZZ[\zeta_p]$, then $\a/n=\sum_i a_i/n \zeta_p^i$. Now, as $\a/n \in \ZZ[\zeta_p]$, pick the basis of $\ZZ[\zeta_p]$ which does not contain $\zeta_p$ (which is possible as any subset of $\{1,\zeta_p,\dots,\zeta_p^{p-1}\}$ with $p-1$ elements forms a basis of $\ZZ[\zeta_p]$.). Then $\a=\sum_i b_i \zeta_p^i$ where $b_i \in \ZZ$. Therefore comparing coefficients, we get the result.

nodes.statement: Let $p \geq 3$ be an prime number, $\zeta_p$ a $p$-th root of unity and $ \a \in \ZZ[\zeta_p]$. Then since by \ref{lem:flt_ideals_coprime} we know the ideals are coprime, then by lemma \ref{lemma:ideals_mult_to_power} we have that each $(x+y\zeta_p^i)=\gotha^p$, for $\gotha$ some ideal. Note that, $[\gotha^p]=1$ in the class group. Now, since $p$ does not divide the size of the class group we have that $[\gotha]=1$ in the class group, so its principal. So we have $x+y\zeta_p^i=u_i\a_i^p$ with $u_i$ a unit. So by \ref{lem:exists_int_sum_eq_zero} we have some $k$ such that $x+y\zeta_p-\zeta_p^{2k}x-\zeta_p^{2k-1}y \equiv 0 \pmod p$. If $1,\zeta_p,\zeta_p^{2k},\zeta_p^{2k-1}$ are distinct, then \ref{lem:dvd_coeff_cycl_integer} says that (since $p \geq 5$) $p$ divides $x,y$, contrary to our assumption. So they cannot be distinct, but checking each case leads to a contradiction, therefore there cannot be any such solutions.

nodes.statement: By our assumptions we have the following equality of ideals in $\ZZ[\zeta_p]$: \[ \prod_{k=0}^{p-1} (x+\zeta_p^ky) = \mathfrak{p}^{pm}\mathfrak{a}^p, \] where $\mathfrak{a}=(z)$, $\mathfrak{p}=(1-\zeta_p)$ (which is prime) and $m=n(p-1)$. Now as $mp \geq p$ we must have that at least one of the terms on the lhs is divisible by $\mathfrak{p}$. Note that since \[x+\zeta_p^iy= x+\zeta_p^ky - \zeta_p^k(1-\zeta_p^{i-k})y\] it follows every $x+\zeta_p^k$ is divisible by $\mathfrak{p}$ for $0 \le k \le p-1$. This proves the first claim. For the second claim, we begin by observing that if $x+\zeta_p^ky \equiv x + \zeta_p^i y \mod \mathfrak{p}^2$ (for $0 \leq k < i \leq p-1$) then $\zeta_p^ky(1-\zeta_p^{i-k}) \equiv 0 \mod \mathfrak{p}^2$ which cannot happen as $y$ is coprime to $\mathfrak{p}$. Therefore since, for $0 \leq k \leq p-1$, $x+\zeta_p^ky$ are all distinct modulo $\mathfrak{p}^2$ we must have that $\frac{x+\zeta_p^k}{1-\zeta_p}$ are non-congruent modulo $\mathfrak{p}$. The second claim now follows by noting that (since $N(\mathfrak{p})=p$), the numbers $\frac{x+\zeta_p^k}{1-\zeta_p}$ form a complete set of residues modulo $\mathfrak{p}$, so one must be divisible by $\mathfrak{p}$.

nodes.name: Conjugates
nodes.statement: Next, let $\a_i=\sigma_i(\zeta_p)$ denote the conjugates of $\zeta_p$, which is the same as the image of $\zeta_p$ under one of the embeddings $\sigma_i: \QQ(\zeta_p) \to \CC$. Now by Proposition \ref{lemma:disc_of_prim_elt_basis} we have \begin{align*}\Delta(\{1,\zeta_p,\dots,\zeta_p^{p-2}\})=\prod_{i < j} (\a_i-\a_j)^2 &=\prod_{i < j} ((1-\a_i)-(1-\a_j))^2\\&=\Delta(\{1,\lam_p,\dots,\lam_p^{p-2}\})\end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Conjugates; translate invariance of the Vandermonde product gives equal discriminants

nodes.name: Apply the norm-of-derivative formula and simplify the sign
nodes.statement: Now, by Proposition \ref{lemma:num_field_disc_in_terms_of_norm}, we have \[\Delta(\{1,\zeta_p,\cdots,\zeta_p^{p-2}\})=(-1)^{\frac{(p-1)(p-2)}{2}}N_{K/\QQ}(\Phi_p'(\zeta_p) )\] Since $p$ is odd $(-1)^{\frac{(p-1)(p-2)}{2}}=(-1)^{\frac{(p-1)}{2}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the norm-of-derivative formula and simplify the sign

nodes.name: Compute $\Phi_p'(\zeta_p)$
nodes.statement: Next, we see that \[\Phi_p'(x)=\frac{px^{p-1}(x-1)-(x^p-1)}{(x-1)^2}\] therefore \[\Phi_p'(\zeta_p)=-\frac{p\zeta_p^{p-1}}{\lam_p}.\]

nodes.name: Norms of $\zeta_p$ and $\lambda_p$
nodes.statement: Lastly, note that $N_{K/\QQ}(\zeta_p)=1$, since this is the constant term in its minimal polynomial. Similarly, we see $N_{K/\QQ}(\lam_p)=p$.

nodes.name: Combine the norms
nodes.statement: Putting this all together, we get \[N_{K/\QQ}(\Phi_p'(\zeta_p) )=\frac{N_{K/\QQ}(p)N_{K\QQ}(\zeta_p)^{p-1}}{N_{K/\QQ}(-\lam_p)}=(-1)^{p-1}p^{p-2}=p^{p-2}\]

nodes.name: Reduce to $\OO_K\subseteq\ZZ[\zeta_p]$
nodes.statement: We need to prove is that $\OO_K=\ZZ[\zeta_p]$. The inclusion $\ZZ[\zeta_p] \subseteq \OO_K$ is obvious.

nodes.name: Discriminant lemmas give $p^kx\in\ZZ[\zeta_p]$
nodes.statement: Let now $x \in \OO_K$. By Lemma \ref{lemma:disc_int_basis} and Proposition \ref{lem:discr_of_cyclo}, there is $k \in \NN$ such that $p^k x \in \ZZ[\zeta_p]$.

nodes.name: Conclude with the Eisenstein criterion lemma
nodes.statement: We conclude by Lemma \ref{lemma:eis_crit_and_alg_ints}.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude with the Eisenstein criterion lemma

nodes.name: The unit claim follows from the cited lemma
nodes.statement: Lemma \ref{lemma:zeta_pow_sub_eq_unit_zeta_sub_one} gives that $u$ is a unit.
nodes.statement_short: The unit claim follows from the cited lemma
nodes.section: 4 Fermat's Last Theorem for regular primes

nodes.name: Reduce to coprimality
nodes.statement: So all that needs to be proved is that the ideals are coprime.
nodes.section: 4 Fermat's Last Theorem for regular primes

nodes.name: Assume a common prime ideal factor
nodes.statement: Assume not, then for some $i \neq j$ we have some prime ideal $\gothp$ dividing by $(x+y\zeta_p^i)$ and $(x+y\zeta_p^j)$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume a common prime ideal factor
nodes.section: 4 Fermat's Last Theorem for regular primes

nodes.name: Sum and difference arguments
nodes.statement: It must then also divide their sum and their difference, so we must have $\gothp | (1-\zeta_p)$ or $\gothp | y$. Similarly, $\gothp$ divides $\zeta_p^j(x+y\zeta_p^i)-\zeta_p^i(x+y\zeta_p^j)$ so $\gothp$ divides $x$ or $(1-\zeta_p)$.
nodes.section: 4 Fermat's Last Theorem for regular primes

nodes.name: Identify the prime as $(1-\zeta_p)$
nodes.statement: We can't have $\gothp$ dividing $x,y$ since they are coprime, therefore $\gothp |(1-\zeta_p)$. We know that since $(1-\zeta_p)$ has norm $p$ it must be a prime ideal, so $\gothp=(1-\zeta_p)$.
nodes.section: 4 Fermat's Last Theorem for regular primes

nodes.name: Derive $p\mid z$, a contradiction
nodes.statement: Now, note that $x+y \equiv x+y\zeta_p^i \equiv 0 \mod \gothp$. But since $x,y \in \ZZ$ this means we would have $x+y \equiv 0 \pmod p$, which implies $z^p \equiv 0 \pmod p$ which contradicts our assumptions.
nodes.section: 4 Fermat's Last Theorem for regular primes

nodes.name: Write $\a/n$ in coefficients
nodes.statement: Looking at $\a=a_0+a_1\zeta_p+\cdots+a_{p-1}\zeta_p^{p-1}$, if one of the $a_i$'s is zero and $\a/n \in \ZZ[\zeta_p]$, then $\a/n=\sum_i a_i/n \zeta_p^i$.
nodes.section: 4 Fermat's Last Theorem for regular primes

nodes.name: Choose a basis avoiding the zero coefficient
nodes.statement: Now, as $\a/n \in \ZZ[\zeta_p]$, pick the basis of $\ZZ[\zeta_p]$ which does not contain $\zeta_p$ (which is possible as any subset of $\{1,\zeta_p,\dots,\zeta_p^{p-1}\}$ with $p-1$ elements forms a basis of $\ZZ[\zeta_p]$.). Then $\a=\sum_i b_i \zeta_p^i$ where $b_i \in \ZZ$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose a basis avoiding the zero coefficient
nodes.section: 4 Fermat's Last Theorem for regular primes

nodes.name: Compare coefficients
nodes.statement: Therefore comparing coefficients, we get the result.
nodes.section: 4 Fermat's Last Theorem for regular primes

nodes.name: Unit lemma and $p$-th power congruence
nodes.statement: Using lemma \ref{lemma:unit_lemma} we have $(x+y\zeta_p^i) =\beta \zeta_p^k \a^p$ which is congruent modulo $p$ to $\beta \zeta_p^k a \pmod p$ for some integer $a$ by \ref{lem:exists_int_sub_pow_prime_dvd}.
nodes.section: 4 Fermat's Last Theorem for regular primes

nodes.name: Take complex conjugates
nodes.statement: Now, if we consider the complex conjugate we have $\ov{(x+y\zeta_p^i) }\equiv \beta \zeta_p^{-k}a \pmod p$.
nodes.section: 4 Fermat's Last Theorem for regular primes

nodes.name: Subtract to get the congruence
nodes.statement: Looking at $(x+y\zeta_p^i)-\zeta_p^{2k}\ov{(x+y\zeta_p^i) }$ then gives the result.
nodes.section: 4 Fermat's Last Theorem for regular primes

nodes.name: Reduce mod $p$ to rule out $x\equiv y\equiv -z$
nodes.statement: The first part is easy. Reducing modulo $p$, using Fermat's little theorem, you get that if $x \equiv y \equiv -z \pmod p$ then $3z \equiv 0 \pmod p$. But since $p >3$ this means $p |z$ but this contradicts $\gcd(xyz,p)=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce mod $p$ to rule out $x\equiv y\equiv -z$
nodes.section: 4 Fermat's Last Theorem for regular primes

nodes.name: Relabel so that $x\not\equiv y$
nodes.statement: Now, if $x \equiv y \pmod p$ then $x \not \equiv -z \pmod p$ we can relabel $y,z$ so that wlog $x \not \equiv y$ (this uses that $p$ is odd).
nodes.section: 4 Fermat's Last Theorem for regular primes

nodes.name: Dispose of $p=3$
nodes.statement: For $p=3$ use the standard elementary arguments, so assume $p \geq 5$.
nodes.section: 4 Fermat's Last Theorem for regular primes

nodes.name: Factor $z^p$ as a product of ideals
nodes.statement: First thing is to note that if $x^p+y^p=z^p$ then \[z^p=(x+y)(x+\zeta_py)\cdots(x+y\zeta_p^{p-1})\] as ideals.
nodes.statement_short: Factor $z^p$ as a product of ideals
nodes.section: 4 Fermat's Last Theorem for regular primes

nodes.name: Coprimality makes each factor a $p$-th power
nodes.statement: Then since by \ref{lem:flt_ideals_coprime} we know the ideals are coprime, then by lemma \ref{lemma:ideals_mult_to_power} we have that each $(x+y\zeta_p^i)=\gotha^p$, for $\gotha$ some ideal.
nodes.statement_short: Coprimality makes each factor a $p$-th power
nodes.section: 4 Fermat's Last Theorem for regular primes

nodes.name: Regularity makes $\gotha$ principal
nodes.statement: Note that, $[\gotha^p]=1$ in the class group. Now, since $p$ does not divide the size of the class group we have that $[\gotha]=1$ in the class group, so its principal. So we have $x+y\zeta_p^i=u_i\a_i^p$ with $u_i$ a unit.
nodes.section: 4 Fermat's Last Theorem for regular primes

nodes.name: Obtain the congruence for some $k$
nodes.statement: So by \ref{lem:exists_int_sum_eq_zero} we have some $k$ such that $x+y\zeta_p-\zeta_p^{2k}x-\zeta_p^{2k-1}y \equiv 0 \pmod p$.
nodes.section: 4 Fermat's Last Theorem for regular primes

nodes.name: Distinct exponents give $p\mid x,y$
nodes.statement: If $1,\zeta_p,\zeta_p^{2k},\zeta_p^{2k-1}$ are distinct, then \ref{lem:dvd_coeff_cycl_integer} says that (since $p \geq 5$) $p$ divides $x,y$, contrary to our assumption.
nodes.section: 4 Fermat's Last Theorem for regular primes

nodes.name: Check remaining cases
nodes.statement: So they cannot be distinct, but checking each case leads to a contradiction, therefore there cannot be any such solutions.
nodes.section: 4 Fermat's Last Theorem for regular primes

nodes.name: Ideal factorization of the equation
nodes.statement: By our assumptions we have the following equality of ideals in $\ZZ[\zeta_p]$: \[ \prod_{k=0}^{p-1} (x+\zeta_p^ky) = \mathfrak{p}^{pm}\mathfrak{a}^p, \] where $\mathfrak{a}=(z)$, $\mathfrak{p}=(1-\zeta_p)$ (which is prime) and $m=n(p-1)$.
nodes.section: 4 Fermat's Last Theorem for regular primes

nodes.name: Some factor is divisible by $\mathfrak{p}$
nodes.statement: Now as $mp \geq p$ we must have that at least one of the terms on the lhs is divisible by $\mathfrak{p}$.
nodes.section: 4 Fermat's Last Theorem for regular primes

nodes.name: All factors are divisible by $\mathfrak{p}$
nodes.statement: Note that since \[x+\zeta_p^iy= x+\zeta_p^ky - \zeta_p^k(1-\zeta_p^{i-k})y\] it follows every $x+\zeta_p^k$ is divisible by $\mathfrak{p}$ for $0 \le k \le p-1$. This proves the first claim.
nodes.section: 4 Fermat's Last Theorem for regular primes

nodes.name: Factors are distinct modulo $\mathfrak{p}^2$
nodes.statement: For the second claim, we begin by observing that if $x+\zeta_p^ky \equiv x + \zeta_p^i y \mod \mathfrak{p}^2$ (for $0 \leq k < i \leq p-1$) then $\zeta_p^ky(1-\zeta_p^{i-k}) \equiv 0 \mod \mathfrak{p}^2$ which cannot happen as $y$ is coprime to $\mathfrak{p}$. Therefore since, for $0 \leq k \leq p-1$, $x+\zeta_p^ky$ are all distinct modulo $\mathfrak{p}^2$ we must have that $\frac{x+\zeta_p^k}{1-\zeta_p}$ are non-congruent modulo $\mathfrak{p}$.
nodes.section: 4 Fermat's Last Theorem for regular primes

nodes.name: Complete residue system gives the unique $i_0$
nodes.statement: The second claim now follows by noting that (since $N(\mathfrak{p})=p$), the numbers $\frac{x+\zeta_p^k}{1-\zeta_p}$ form a complete set of residues modulo $\mathfrak{p}$, so one must be divisible by $\mathfrak{p}$.
nodes.statement_short: Complete residue system gives the unique $i_0$
nodes.section: 4 Fermat's Last Theorem for regular primes

nodes.name: Construct $\beta$ from $\gamma$
nodes.statement: Pick some $\gamma \in K$ and consider \[\beta=\gamma \a+ \sigma(\gamma)\a \sigma(\a)+\cdots+\sigma^{n-1}(\gamma)\a \sigma(\a)\cdots \sigma^{n-1}(\a),\] where $[K/F]=n$.

nodes.name: Verify $\a\sigma(\beta)=\beta$
nodes.statement: Since the norm $\a$ is $1$ then we have $\a \sigma(\a)\cdots \sigma^{n-1}(\a)=1$ from which one verifies that $\a \sigma(\beta)=\beta$. This also uses that since we know that Galois group is cyclic, all the embeddings are given by $\sigma^i$.

nodes.name: Linear independence of embeddings gives $\beta\neq0$
nodes.statement: Note that $ \a+ \sigma\a \sigma(\a)+\cdots+\sigma^{n-1}\a \sigma(\a)\cdots \sigma^{n-1}(\a)$ is a linear combination of the embeddings $\sigma^i$. Now, using \ref{lem:lin_indep_iff_disc_ne_zero} we can check that they must be linearly independent. Therefore, it is possible to find a $\gamma$ such that $\beta \neq 0$.

nodes.name: Conclude and clear denominators
nodes.statement: Putting everything together we have found $\a=\beta/\sigma(\beta)$. Using \ref{lem:exists_alg_int} we see that its possible to make sure $\beta \in \OO_K$ as required.

nodes.name: Case of higher congruence: local lifting gives splitting
nodes.statement: Suppose that we have $\xi = \a_0^p \mod \lam_p^{p+1}$. The using \ref{lem:loc_ramification} with $m=p-1,r=2$ gives an $\a$ such that $\a^p=\xi$ in $\OO_{F_\gothp}^\times$. Meaning that $(\lam_p)$ is split in the local extension and hence split in $K/F$ (note: add this lemma explicitly somewhere).
nodes.statement_short: Case of higher congruence: local lifting gives splitting

nodes.name: Case of exact congruence: compute the different of an explic
nodes.statement: If we instead have $\lam_p^p \parallel (\xi-\a_0^p)$, then pick some element in $ K$ which agrees with $\a_0$ up to $\lam_p^{p+1}$, which we again call $\a_0$ and consider \[\eta= (\sqrt[p]{\xi}-\a_0)/\lam_p\] so that $K=F(\eta)$. Now, if $m_\eta$ is the minimal monic polynomial for $\eta$ then by definition it follows that \[m_\eta(x) \equiv x^p+\left (\a_0^{p-1}p/\lam_p^{p-1} \right )x+ (\a_0^p-\xi)/\lam_p^p \mod \lam_p\] So in fact $\eta \in \OO_K$. Now, if we look at $m_\eta'$ we see that $m_\eta'(\eta)$ is coprime to $\lam_p$ and therefore coprime to $\gothd_{K/F}$ (by \ref{lem:diff_ideal_eqn}) and therefore $\lam_p$ is unramified (by \ref{lem:diff_ram}).
nodes.statement_short: Case of exact congruence: compute the different of an explicit generator

nodes.name: Introduce $\eta$
nodes.statement: If we instead have $\lam_p^p \parallel (\xi-\a_0^p)$, then pick some element in $ K$ which agrees with $\a_0$ up to $\lam_p^{p+1}$, which we again call $\a_0$ and consider \[\eta= (\sqrt[p]{\xi}-\a_0)/\lam_p\] so that $K=F(\eta)$.

nodes.name: Minimal polynomial of $\eta$ shows integrality
nodes.statement: Now, if $m_\eta$ is the minimal monic polynomial for $\eta$ then by definition it follows that \[m_\eta(x) \equiv x^p+\left (\a_0^{p-1}p/\lam_p^{p-1} \right )x+ (\a_0^p-\xi)/\lam_p^p \mod \lam_p\] So in fact $\eta \in \OO_K$.

nodes.name: Derivative coprime to $\lambda_p$ so unramified
nodes.statement: Now, if we look at $m_\eta'$ we see that $m_\eta'(\eta)$ is coprime to $\lam_p$ and therefore coprime to $\gothd_{K/F}$ (by \ref{lem:diff_ideal_eqn}) and therefore $\lam_p$ is unramified (by \ref{lem:diff_ram}).

nodes.name: Assume $u$ not a $p$-th power
nodes.statement: Assume $u$ is not a $p$-th power. Then let $K=F(\sqrt[p]{u})$ and $\eta \in K$ be as in \ref{lem:Hilbert92}. Then $K/F$ is Galois and cyclic of degree $p$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume $u$ not a $p$-th power; set up the Kummer extension

nodes.name: Apply Hilbert 90
nodes.statement: Now by Hilbert 90 (\ref{Hilbert90}) we can find $\beta \in \OO_K$ such that \[\eta = \beta/\sigma(\beta)\] (but note that by our assumption $\beta$ is not a unit).

nodes.name: Unramified so $(\beta)$ descends to $\gothb$
nodes.statement: Note that the ideal $(\eta)$ is invariant under $\Gal(K/F)$ by construction and by \ref{lem:ramification_lem} it cannot be ramified, therefore $(\beta)$ is the extension of scalars of some ideal $\gothb$ in $\OO_F$.

nodes.name: If $\gothb$ principal, contradiction with Hilbert 92
nodes.statement: Now if $\gothb$ is principal generated by some $\gamma$ then $\beta=v \gamma$ for some $v \in \OO_K^\times$. But this means that \[\eta = \beta/\sigma(\beta)= v/(\sigma(v)) \cdot \gamma / \sigma(\gamma)=v/\sigma(v) \] contradicting our assumption coming from \ref{lem:Hilbert92}.

nodes.name: Otherwise $p$ divides the class number
nodes.statement: On the other hand, $\gothb^p= N_{K/F}(\beta)$ is principal, meaning $p$ divides the class group of $F$ as required.
